terms.comment: From summa, the main points. Seneca says it was the Latin word, and breviārium the one people used in his day.

terms.gloss: an abridgment, an epitome (of a book)
terms.comment: A Greek word, used by Cicero of a shortened version of a longer work; also epitoma, epitomae f. (Cic. Att. 12.5.3).

evidence: Sen. Ep. 39.1; Suet. (Lewis & Short, s.v. breviārius)
terms.comment: Post-Augustan; the everyday word of Seneca’s time, by his own account.

evidence: Cic. Att. 5.16.1: aliquid summātim perscrībere; Varr. RR 2 praef. 6: breviter ac summātim percurram (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To give the gist: summātim nārrāre, perscrībere.

evidence: Cic. Att. 14.1.1; Off. 1.149 (Lewis & Short, s.v. summa)
terms.comment: “In a word”, closing a list or an argument.

phrases.latin: ōrātiō, quae nunc vulgō breviārium dīcitur, ōlim, cum Latīnē loquerēmur, summārium vocābātur
phrases.english: the kind of piece now commonly called a breviarium was once, when we spoke Latin, called a summarium

phrases.latin: Ita vīdistī summātim rēs omnēs, quae ostendī poterunt
phrases.english: So you have seen, in brief, all the things that could be shown
